questions.question: When two kinds of living things live closely together for a long time, biologists call it symbiosis, and they sort every case into one of three types. What decides which type a case belongs to?
questions.answer: Whether each is helped, harmed or neither
choices: Whether each is helped, harmed or neither
Which of the two kinds is the larger
Whether the two are plants, animals or both
How closely related the two kinds are
questions.context: The three types are sorted by what each partner gets. In mutualism both gain; in commensalism one gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed; in parasitism one gains at the other's cost. Partners can be large or small, plant, animal or fungus, close kin or not.
questions.grade_note: Symbiosis and its three kinds, told apart by who benefits and who is harmed, are the core of the 6th-grade line on relationships between species (TEKS 6.12B).

questions.question: A honeybee lands on a flower and drinks its nectar. Pollen dusts the hairs on its body, and at the next flower it visits, some of that pollen rubs off. What kind of interaction is this between the bee and the plant?
choices: Mutualism
Commensalism
Parasitism
Predation
questions.context: Both sides gain, so it is mutualism. The bee gets food from the flower, and the plant gets its pollen carried to another flower, which lets it make seeds. The bee is no parasite, since the plant gains as well.
questions.grade_note: Bees and flowers are the standard 6th-grade example of mutualism, where the simple why is pollination.

questions.question: Trillions of bacteria live in a healthy person's gut, and many of them do the person good. What do they do for the person?
questions.answer: They digest fibre the body cannot
choices: They digest fibre the body cannot
They make the acid in the stomach
They make the bile that breaks up fat
They squeeze the food along the gut
questions.context: Bacteria in the large intestine break down fibre that a person's own body cannot digest, and many make vitamins such as vitamin K. They get a home and a share of the food that reaches them, so both sides gain: mutualism. Stomach acid comes from the stomach's own lining, bile from the liver, and the squeezing that moves food along comes from the muscles of the gut wall.
questions.grade_note: The helpful bacteria in the human gut are a 6th-grade example of mutualism, and the job they do is its simple why.

questions.question: A tapeworm fastens itself to the inside wall of a person's gut. The person is its host, and the worm seldom kills its host. Why not?
questions.answer: It needs a living host to feed and spread
choices: It needs a living host to feed and spread
It takes only food its host does not need
It leaves when its host begins to weaken
It helps its host digest food in return
questions.context: A tapeworm soaks up nutrients from the food its host digests, and its eggs leave the host's body to reach new hosts, so it cannot live on without a living host. A host killed quickly would leave the worm no time to spread. It takes food the host needs, stays fastened for years and gives nothing back, which is what makes it a parasite.
questions.grade_note: Why a parasite seldom kills its host, since it needs the living host to feed and to spread, is the simple why behind parasitism in the 6th-grade line, and the tapeworm is named in the unit's scope.

questions.question: Pea, bean and clover plants grow small lumps on their roots, each one packed with bacteria. The plant and the bacteria both gain from the partnership. What do the bacteria give the plant?
choices: Nitrogen taken from the air
Sugar broken out of rotting leaves
Water drawn from deep soil
Oxygen drawn from the soil
questions.context: Air is mostly nitrogen gas, which plants need but cannot use as it is. The bacteria in the lumps turn it into a form the plant can take up, and the plant pays them with sugar made in its own leaves; bacteria that rot dead leaves free minerals, not sugar. Farmers long grew such plants to keep their soil rich.
questions.grade_note: Bacteria in the root lumps of peas and beans are a common 6th-grade mutualism example, and what each side gets is its simple why.

questions.question: An orchid grows high on the branch of a rainforest tree, far above the dim forest floor. Its roots cling to the bark and soak up rain and mist. What kind of interaction is this between the orchid and the tree?
choices: Commensalism
Parasitism
Mutualism
Competition
questions.context: The orchid gains a place in the light, and the tree is neither helped nor harmed: commensalism. It is no parasite, since it takes no water or food from inside the tree. Biologists add that proving a host is truly unaffected is hard, since small costs or benefits can go unseen.
questions.grade_note: Commensalism, where one partner gains and the other is unaffected, is the second kind of symbiosis in the 6th-grade line, and plants growing on trees are its usual example.

questions.question: A tick climbs onto a deer and bites into its skin. For several days it drinks the deer's blood, and then it drops to the ground, swollen. What kind of interaction is this?
choices: Parasitism
Predation
Commensalism
Mutualism
questions.context: The tick gains a meal and the deer loses blood, and a heavy load of ticks can wear an animal down: one gains at the other's cost, so it is parasitism. It is not predation, since a predator kills and eats its prey, while a parasite usually feeds on a host that lives on.
questions.grade_note: Parasitism, and how a parasite differs from a predator, is part of the 6th-grade line on relationships between species; the tick is a standard example.

questions.question: Mistletoe grows on the branches of trees, and its green leaves make some of its own food from sunlight. Even so, biologists call it a parasite of the tree. Why?
questions.answer: It grows into the branch to take water
choices: It grows into the branch to take water
It coils around the branch to choke it
It drips poison onto the bark to rot it
It soaks up rain that falls on the tree
questions.context: A root-like part of the mistletoe grows into the branch and draws off water and minerals the tree carries up from its roots. Making some of its own food does not stop it being a parasite: it gains at the tree's cost, and a heavy load can stunt a tree or even kill it.
questions.grade_note: Mistletoe is a named 6th-grade example of parasitism, and its why corrects the belief that a green plant cannot be a parasite.

questions.question: The Hudson's Bay Company counted the lynx furs that trappers sold it, year after year, for close to a century, and records of snowshoe hares cover the same years. Both numbers rose and fell about every ten years. When did the lynx numbers usually peak?
questions.answer: A year or two after the hares peaked
choices: A year or two after the hares peaked
A year or two before the hares peaked
In the same year as the hares peaked
When the hares were at their fewest
questions.context: Lynx live mostly on snowshoe hares, so their numbers can climb only once the hares have grown plentiful. The predator's peaks trail the prey's by one to two years, across a cycle of about ten years.
questions.grade_note: Predator and prey numbers rising and falling together, with the predator a step behind, is the predator-prey part of the 6th-grade line, and the lynx and hare are its textbook case.

questions.question: Snowshoe hares are most of what lynx eat, and in some years the lynx catch so many that hares become rare across the forest. Yet the hares never die out. What keeps them from dying out?
questions.answer: As hares grow scarce, lynx grow fewer too
choices: As hares grow scarce, lynx grow fewer too
Hares hide in burrows lynx cannot reach
Lynx stop hunting until hares recover
A sickness kills off lynx every ten years
questions.context: With few hares to catch, many lynx starve and few of their kittens survive, so the hunters grow scarce too. With fewer lynx about, the hares that are left can breed back up, and the cycle begins again. Food for the hares plays a part as well, and snowshoe hares rest in shallow hollows, not burrows.
questions.grade_note: Why predator and prey numbers rise and fall together, and so why a predator seldom wipes out its prey, is the simple why behind the 6th-grade predator-prey line.

316e3aa25b.why: Judge (medium tell): the stem named mutualism and parasitism, whose plain meanings give the sorting rule away. The names are taken out of the stem; the key, the three wrong choices and the teaching context are unchanged, and 'types' now names the three kinds so it is not confused with the two kinds of living things.

2cce2fac53.why: Judge (medium tell): 'They carry oxygen into the blood' was not a live choice for gut bacteria. It is replaced by 'They squeeze the food along the gut', the job of the gut's own muscles (F31). Fact-check note taken: bile breaks up fat (emulsifies it, F32) rather than digesting it, so that choice now says 'breaks up fat'. Context updated to match. Stem and key unchanged.

0a83478dc5.why: Judge (low tell): 'Sugar made from sunlight' was struck by the stem, since the bacteria live in root lumps in the dark. It is replaced by 'Sugar broken out of rotting leaves', live from the decomposer idea and false (decomposers free minerals, not sugar; F33). Fact-check note taken: farmers did not know the soil gain was nitrogen, so the last sentence says 'rich'. Stem and key unchanged.

789733bc41.why: Judge (low tell): 'but never grow into the tree' struck Parasitism outright and pointed at the mistletoe question's key. The clause is cut, so the belief that a plant on a tree is a parasite (M2) is a live choice; the key still follows, since the orchid takes its water from rain and mist. Choices and context unchanged.

3099952515.why: Fact-check error: the context counted Lyme disease as a cost to the deer, but deer do not get Lyme disease (dead-end hosts; F29). It now says a heavy load of ticks can wear an animal down (energy loss, anaemia; F29). Judge (low): 'while the deer walks on' struck Predation, the lure the point depends on, so it is cut. Choices and key unchanged.

cf9da7e256.why: Fact-check uncertain: the stem said the Company kept records of hare furs sold to it for close to a century, but the classic hare series is fur records only for 1844-1904 and questionnaires for 1905-1935 (F30). The stem now says the Company counted lynx furs and that hare records cover the same years. Choices, key and context unchanged.

dropped.question: A lichen spreads like a crust of grey-green paint over a bare rock. It is a fungus and a green alga living together as one. What does the alga give the fungus?
dropped.why: Judge (medium tell): the alga's gift, food made from sunlight, follows from facts the bank already teaches (green algae make food from sunlight, T1; fungi cannot, T2 one-cell-or-many), so the lichen fact is never needed. The judge's fix (ask what the fungus gives) has the same flaw: those same facts strike its 'food from sunlight' and 'oxygen' lures. The unit also had four mutualism items, three in this 'what does A give B' shape, and nothing on why a parasite seldom kills its host; a parasitism question on that scope line takes its place.
